open-question.question: Does the open-question tool gain a multi-block form of embed --recommendation that writes several blocks from one standard-input message and prints each accepted block's lifted line, or does the batched shell call keep the existing one-block embed process and a separate lift per block with the tool unchanged? If the tool changes, whether a refused block in the batch leaves the valid blocks written, and what the tool prints per accepted block, hinge on that choice.
open-question.recommendation: The milestone's saving is in orchestrator turns, which the one-block process already brings to the two-call floor; a multi-block or lift-printing form would buy only call-text lines at the cost of a delimiter grammar, new tests, and a break in the silent-mutator and document-unchanged-on-failure contract, while leaving the alternatives batch on the one-block shape it already ships.
open-question.alternative: The open-question tool, its tests, and its contract stay as they are. The batched shell call runs one `embed --recommendation` process per picked block, each with its own quoted heredoc, and then one separate `lift` per block whose embed succeeded. A refused block is refused by its own process with the document unchanged for that block, while the other blocks' processes still write. No new flag, subcommand, or output shape is added. It adds no code, no tests, and no exception to the tool's contract (a mutator prints nothing on success, and a failure is one Error line with the document unchanged). The goal already names this per-process shape as the baseline, and it gives per-block refusal isolation with no new mechanism. The whole change is confined to the skill's prose, the docs, and the rebuilt trees. The call's text still carries one full embed command line and one lift line per block, so a 16-block run writes 32 tool invocations into one call. Holding only the successful blocks' lifted lines for the commit body is left entirely to shell logic inside the call, which is the sibling Commit body capture question's to settle.

The tool keeps one block per `embed` process but gains an opt-in flag on `embed --recommendation` that, on success, prints the written block's lifted line (`<option> — <rationale>`, exactly as `lift` would print it) to standard output. Refusal is unchanged: one Error line on stderr, exit 1, the document unchanged. The batched call runs one embed heredoc per block with the flag and no separate `lift`. There is no multi-block form. Each block still gets its own process, so a refused block leaves the valid blocks written with no new partial-write logic. The separate lift per block disappears, and the lifted line comes out only from an embed that succeeded, so a refused block contributes no body line by construction. The tool change is small: one flag that reuses the existing lift rendering, with tests added beside the 72 existing embed tests. It makes a scoped exception to the "a mutator prints nothing on success" contract that `tests/test_contract.py` enforces, and that exception has to be stated and tested. It also saves less than a multi-block form: the call still carries one embed command and one heredoc per block, so the text of a 16-block call shrinks only by the 16 lift lines.

`embed --recommendation` gains a multi-block form. One standard-input message carries the recommendation-half fragments of several blocks, each wrapped in a delimiter that names its Short Title. The tool validates each block's fragment independently. It writes every valid block in one canonical rewrite of the document and leaves each refused block exactly as it stood. It prints the lifted line of each accepted block to standard output and reports each refused block on stderr, exiting non-zero when any block was refused. It shortens the call the most: one embed command and one heredoc for the whole batch, with the commit body coming straight from the tool's stdout and no lift calls. It keeps the goal's property that every valid block lands while each refused block reports on its own, and the document is rewritten once rather than once per block. It is the largest tool change. It needs a new delimiter grammar (the current fragment rule refuses any `<open-question>` line) and new tests, and it breaks two contract rules at once: it prints on success, and it changes the document while still exiting with a failure, emitting possibly several Error lines rather than exactly one. How each refusal line is paired with its block depends on the sibling Refused block print pairing question.

`embed --recommendation` gains the same multi-block form: one standard-input message carrying several blocks' fragments, each delimited by its Short Title, each validated independently. Every valid block is written in one rewrite, and each refused block is left unchanged and reported on stderr. On success it prints nothing, as every mutator does today, so the batched call still runs one `lift` per accepted block afterwards to build the commit body. It collapses the per-block embed commands and heredocs into one while keeping the "a mutator prints nothing on success" half of the contract intact. Valid blocks still land beside refused ones, as the goal describes. The call keeps one lift line per block, and it must tell which blocks were accepted in order to lift only those. That pushes acceptance tracking into shell logic or into parsing the tool's stderr, which interacts with the sibling Commit body capture and Refused block print pairing questions. It also still departs from the contract's "document unchanged on failure" rule whenever a batch is partly refused.

`embed --recommendation` gains a multi-block form that validates every block in the one standard-input message before writing anything. If any block is refused, the whole call is refused with the document unchanged and nothing written. If every block is valid, all are written in one rewrite and the lifted line of each is printed to standard output. A refusal means the runner corrects the refused fragment and re-sends the whole batch. It preserves the tool's write-once-or-never atomicity and its "document unchanged on failure" rule, so a refusal never leaves the document half-annotated. It still collapses the batch to one embed and one heredoc with the commit body on stdout. It contradicts the goal's stated shape, in which each refused block prints its own Error line while the rest land and commit, so choosing it means revising the goal first. One rendering slip holds back every valid block, so the corrected call re-sends the whole set rather than only the refused blocks. It also still prints on success, against the mutator contract.

`embed --recommendation` gains a multi-block form that validates every block in one standard-input message and either writes all of them in one rewrite or, if any is refused, writes none and leaves the document unchanged. It prints nothing on success. The batched call runs one `lift` per block after the embed succeeds. It is the only multi-block form that keeps the tool's whole contract unchanged: a mutator prints nothing on success, and a failure leaves the document unchanged. Because every lift follows an all-succeeded embed, the commit body needs no per-block acceptance tracking. Like the printing all-or-nothing form, it contradicts the goal's statement that valid blocks land while refused ones report, so the goal would need revising. Any slip re-sends the whole batch. It also keeps the per-block lift lines, so it shortens the call less than either printing multi-block form.

open-question.question: Within the one batched shell call, in what form are the lifted lines of the blocks whose embed succeeded held between the lift calls and the git commit that records them as the Recommendation-annotation body, so that a refused block contributes no line and the rule against holding a tool command or a path list in a shell variable is respected?
open-question.recommendation: It is the goal's own per-block embed-then-lift shape: the lift runs only inside the branch an exit-0 embed opens, so a refused block adds no line without any spurious lift or discarded stderr, the body reaches git through the commit procedure's own second -m, and conditioning the annotation commit on a non-empty body is what keeps a zero-block call from committing an empty-bodied annotation; the value is one quoted text value set and used within the one call, never a tool command or a path list.
open-question.alternative: Carrier: one quoted shell variable, set empty at the top of the call and grown inside it. Gating: each block's `lift` runs only when that block's `embed --recommendation` exited 0 (an `if embed …; then … fi` around it), and its printed line is appended to the variable with an explicit newline join, so a refused block never reaches `lift` and adds nothing. Timing: the lift follows its own embed, block by block, as the goal describes. Commit: after the dirty-own-path guard and the path-scoped `git add`, `git commit -q -m "Recommendation-annotation: <milestone_id>" -m "$body"`, the commit procedure's own `-m "<BODY>"` form. The variable is set and used within the one call and holds text lines, never a tool command or a path list. It maps one to one onto the commit procedure's SUBJECT-plus-BODY form and onto the per-block embed-then-lift order the goal states, and it sits inside the scoping CLAUDE.md already grants the alternatives batch's loop variables (one quoted value, set and used within the one call), so no new carrier, file, or argument to the shell-literalness invariant is needed. It stretches that scoping: unlike the alternatives loop's per-file values, this one value accumulates many lines across the whole call, so the invariant's wording and the CLAUDE.md bullet have to be extended to cover it; command substitution strips trailing newlines, so the join must be written carefully in shell-neutral form (the call runs under zsh as well as bash); and a `lift` that fails after an accepted embed silently drops that block's line unless the call also prints it.

Carrier: a temporary file created by `mktemp` at the top of the call, its single path held in one quoted variable for the call's length (the shape of the capture skill's snapshot), outside the repository so no path-scoped add can reach it. Gating: each block's `lift` runs only when its `embed --recommendation` exited 0, its stdout appended to the file, so a refused block appends nothing. Timing: the lift follows its own embed, block by block. Commit: after the guard and the path-scoped `git add`, the body is read back from the file into the commit (`-m "$(cat …)"` beside the subject). The file is left for the system's temp handling, with no delete step in the call. Each lifted line lands on disk exactly as `lift` printed it, newline included, with no string joining in the shell, and the body survives a failed or interrupted commit as an inspectable file instead of vanishing with the shell. It adds a file with a lifetime and a held path to a pass that today owns no scratch location, so the runner prose gains a temp file the recommendation pass never had, and the body still travels through a command substitution at commit time; the leftover file is a new artifact in a headless chain that a no-delete rule then leaves behind on every run.

Carrier: none — nothing is held between a lift and the commit. Gating: no per-block bookkeeping; after every embed of the call has run, the commit's body is one command substitution that runs `lift` for every block the call sent, with each lift's stderr discarded, and the tool's own refusal is the filter: a block whose embed was refused carries no `<recommendation>`, so its `lift` fails and prints nothing to stdout. Timing: all lifts run together at the commit, after the guard and the path-scoped `git add`, not after each embed. A re-send call lists only the blocks it re-sends, so a block annotated by an earlier call is never lifted twice. It rejects the premise that the lines need holding at all: no variable, no file, and no embed-status branching, so the batched call stays the shortest and plainly within the shell-literalness invariant, and correctness rests on the tool's tested contract that `lift` fails on a block with no recommendation. It departs from the goal's per-block embed-then-lift order; every Short Title is written twice in the call (once on its embed, once in the body substitution), and discarding lift's stderr also hides a genuine lift failure; if the sibling choice on the multi-block embed tool form makes the tool print each accepted block's lifted line itself, there is no separate `lift` to run at commit time and this option's filter does not apply.

open-question.question: When an embed inside the batched call refuses a block, does the call print the tool's Error: line paired with that block's Short Title, or the tool's stderr as it comes, given that some Error: lines (a fragment with no closing recommendation line, for example) name no block?
open-question.recommendation: The likeliest slips are the two fragment-slicing refusals, whose Error lines name no block, so only a shell-side pairing makes every refusal attributable in the same turn with no tool change; the per-block branch it needs is the one the body capture already opens around each embed, and the line shape is the milestone 43 batch's, so the two batch calls read alike.
open-question.alternative: The batched call captures each embed's stderr into one quoted value per block (2>&1 inside a command substitution, set and used within the call) and, when an embed exits non-zero, prints one line per refused block: the block's Short Title, a tab, then the tool's Error: line. Accepted blocks print nothing of their own. The open-question tool is unchanged, and the same pairing covers every refusal class, whether or not the Error: line names the block. Every refusal is attributable from one print with no extra turn and no tool change, including the fragment-slicing refusals ("no <applied-principle>, <depends-on>, or <recommendation> line to extract from", "no </recommendation> line to extract to") that name no block, and it reuses the exact line shape and capture idiom the milestone 43 alternatives batch (provide-alternatives-to-all-open-questions step 3d) already ships, so the two batch calls read alike. The call grows a capture-and-branch per block (an if around each embed's command substitution plus a printf), lengthening the fixed script the runner must reproduce exactly, and on refusals whose Error: line already names the block (a state refusal quoting the open-question id) the title is printed twice.

Each embed runs with its stderr unredirected and uncaptured, so the call prints the tool's Error: lines exactly as the tool emits them, with nothing added to pair them with a block; the call does nothing else to identify the refused set, and the runner attributes each line itself, from the open-question id the line quotes where it names one and, where it names none, by checking afterwards (for example with a list --without-recommendation call in a later turn) which of its picked blocks still lack a recommendation. The tool is unchanged. The shortest possible script: each embed is the bare heredoc call with no capture, branch, or printf, so there is the least for the runner to reproduce and nothing extra to get wrong in the fixed command. The fragment-slicing refusals, the likeliest rendering slip, name no block, so with more than one refusal the runner cannot tell which block a given line belongs to and must spend at least one more tool turn identifying the refused set and may misassign a reason when correcting, eroding the turn saving the milestone exists to capture.

alternative.id: Stderr as it comes plus closing list

open-question.alternative: Each embed's stderr passes through unpaired as in the previous option, and the batched call itself ends (after the embeds, before or alongside its commit) with one list --without-recommendation call whose print names every block still lacking a recommendation, so the refused set arrives in the same output as the raw Error: lines; the runner reconciles the two by itself. The tool is unchanged. The refused set is known from the one call's output with no extra turn, while each embed stays a bare uncaptured call, and the closing list also reports refusals by reading the document rather than by trusting exit statuses. The set is identified but the reasons are not mapped to it: when two or more refusals produce Error: lines that name no block, their order alone ties a line to a block, and the list also prints blocks the run deliberately skipped (no surviving option) and blocks outside this run's pick, which the runner must subtract, so the reconciliation is judgement where pairing would be mechanical.

alternative.id: Tool names the block in every Error line

open-question.alternative: The open-question tool changes so that every Error: line embed --recommendation prints on a block-targeted call names the target block (the fragment-slicing and fragment-validation refusals gain the open-question id the state refusals already quote), still as exactly one Error: line on stderr with exit 1; the batched call then passes each embed's stderr through as it comes, with no pairing in the shell. Attribution lives once in the tool, where it is tested, so the batched script stays as short as the raw-stderr option while every line is still self-identifying, and any other caller of embed (inline single embeds, discuss flows) benefits too. It is a tool change the goal admits only if it earns its place: the reworded refusals break the exact-string assertions in tests/test_embed.py and need both pytest runs and the rebuilt host trees, and the alternatives batch, which already pairs the title, would print it twice unless it changes too or the rewording is limited to --recommendation, leaving the two shapes' messages inconsistent; whether the tool changes at all is also shaped by the Multi-block embed tool form question, under which a multi-block form would have to name each block in its own output anyway.

open-question.question: Does one batched shell call carry every picked block of the run however many there are, or is there a cap on blocks per call above which the run splits the picked set across further calls of the same shape, each committing and sorting?
open-question.applied-principle: Check tier claims against the live environment
open-question.recommendation: Every measured run fits one call with a wide margin (16 blocks at one to two kilobytes each against the 1 MB argument limit getconf ARG_MAX reports on this machine), each embed is its own process so a refusal costs one block and not the batch, and a cap or a runner-judged split would add a number or a discretion no observed run exercises while costing the larger runs the very commits-per-run saving the milestone exists for.
open-question.alternative: One batched shell call carries every picked block of the run, however many there are; the skill states no cap and no splitting rule, so the only further calls a run makes are the corrected re-sends of refused blocks the goal already provides for, each of the same shape and each committing and sorting. Every run reaches the two-turn floor whatever its size and the first call's Recommendation-annotation commit records every block picked in that call; the measured runs topped out at 16 embeds, and a rendered recommendation fragment runs to roughly one to two kilobytes, so even that run's call is a few percent of the 1 MB argument limit on this machine and well inside one turn's output, which seven of twelve runs already spent issuing every embed at once. The call's size grows without bound with the picked set, so an unusually large run (a review pass that surfaced dozens of questions) puts every block into one turn's output and one shell invocation, and a shell-level slip in that text, such as a quoting error or a heredoc terminator collision, costs the whole batch rather than part of it; whether a refusal inside it is cheap to recover depends on how the sibling questions on refusal pairing and second-refusal handling settle.

The skill states a fixed per-call cap set above every observed run (for example around 25 to 30 blocks); a run whose picked set exceeds it splits the set into consecutive calls of the same shape, each embedding, lifting, committing under Recommendation-annotation, and sorting, while every run of the size seen so far stays in one call. It bounds the size and blast radius of a single call against the rare oversized run while leaving every run measured so far at one call and one annotation commit, so the saving the milestone targets is untouched in practice. It adds a number and a splitting rule to the skill and the CLAUDE.md restatement that no measured limit justifies and that ordinary runs never exercise, so the split path stays effectively untested; when it does fire, the run makes several annotation commits and several sorts, and the report step must reconcile commits from several calls, which bears on how the sibling question on the status line source settles.

The skill states a fixed per-call cap inside the range real runs reach (for example around 8 blocks); larger picked sets split into consecutive calls of the same shape, each embedding, lifting, committing under Recommendation-annotation, and sorting, so the larger runs already seen (up to 16 picks) make two or more calls. Each call stays small enough that a shell-level slip or a long run of refusals touches only a bounded slice of the set, and the split path is exercised often enough to stay correct. The largest runs, which held most of the measured excess turns, give back part of the saving the milestone exists for: a 16-pick run spends at least two calls, makes at least two annotation commits splitting its body record, and sorts more than once; the number is a judgment with no measured failure behind it, and the report step must aggregate across calls, which bears on how the sibling question on the status line source settles.

The skill states no number: one call carries every picked block by default, and the runner may split the set into further calls of the same shape, each committing and sorting, when it judges a single call would be too large to write reliably in one turn. It adapts to the actual size of the rendered fragments and to the model running the pass, without committing the skill to a number that may be wrong for some host or model. Splitting becomes prose discretion, so commit counts and turn counts vary between runs and models of the same set, including headless runs where no one sees why a run split, and the skill loses the property of one fixed call run exactly as shown; the report step must still handle several calls, which bears on how the sibling question on the status line source settles.

open-question.question: Is there a limit on how many corrected re-send calls a run makes for blocks the batched call refuses, and what happens to a block still refused when that limit is reached: another corrected call, or a skip reported in the end-of-run advisory?
open-question.recommendation: The goal's "one more call of the same shape" is this bound, it mirrors the alternatives pass's repair-once-then-skip rule so both annotating passes share one robustness contract, and it caps a run at two batch calls and two annotation commits; a block refused twice still carries no recommendation, so the next run re-picks it, and the advisory names it with its second Error line as the one git-absent signal.
open-question.alternative: At most one corrected re-send call per run: every block the first batched call refuses is corrected and re-sent together in one more call of the same shape, and a block that call refuses again is skipped, reported in the end-of-run advisory with its Short Title and that second Error: line verbatim and the remedy of re-running the pass; the run's success line is chosen as usual from what it committed. It mirrors the alternatives pass's repair-once-then-skip rule and design claim 15 (one repair, then a skip, never a run stop), so the two annotating passes share one robustness contract and a run is bounded at two batched calls whatever happens. A block with two independent slips, the second only surfaced once the first is fixed (the tool reports one Error: reason per refusal), is skipped though a further call would have landed it, and the step-7 advisory and its prose gain a second skip kind beside the stale-set skip, with a different remedy.

No limit on corrected re-send calls: every block a batched call refuses is corrected against its Error: line and re-sent in one more call of the same shape, as many times as it takes, so a refused block is never skipped and the step-7 advisory gains no new entry; this keeps the current skill's rule that a refusal is a rendering slip to correct, never a skip. Every pick the run formed reaches the document in the same run, and the rule is the one recommend-all-open-questions already states (step 4: fix the elements and run the same call again), so the skill's prose, the advisory, and design claim 14's unattended-run promise change least. Nothing bounds a runner that keeps misreading the same Error: line, and each extra call now commits and sorts again, so a stuck block can loop a headless run indefinitely and multiply Recommendation-annotation and Question-ordering commits; the measured 61-turn outlier shows the post-decision phase can already run long.

Zero corrected re-send calls: a block the first batched call refuses is not corrected in this run but skipped, its Short Title and the tool's Error: line reported in the end-of-run advisory with the remedy of re-running the pass, which picks it again because it still carries no recommendation. Every run is exactly one batched call with one annotation commit and at most one ordering commit, the simplest and cheapest shape, with no repair loop or per-block tracking in the prose at all. A rendering slip the runner could fix in one turn costs the whole pick: the formed judgment is thrown away and a later run must re-ground and re-pick that block from scratch, and a headless define-to-recommend chain ends with a bare block the answer sweep cannot record.

A small fixed limit above one (two or three corrected re-send calls per run, each carrying every block still refused): a block still refused when the limit is reached is skipped and reported in the end-of-run advisory with its Short Title, its last Error: line verbatim, and the remedy of re-running the pass. Covers the case of a fragment with more than one slip, which the tool reveals one Error: reason at a time, while still guaranteeing the run terminates. The number is arbitrary and diverges from the alternatives pass's one-repair rule, and every extra call commits and sorts again, so a pathological run can land up to four annotation commits for one judgment; the CLAUDE.md and design-claims prose must state and justify a constant no other runner uses.

No fixed count; the limit is progress: the run keeps sending corrected re-send calls while each one is refused for a different reason than before, and a block the next call refuses with the same Error: line it was refused with last time is skipped and reported in the end-of-run advisory with its Short Title, that line verbatim, and the remedy of re-running the pass. Every fixable slip, including several surfaced one at a time, gets fixed in the run, and the only blocks dropped are the ones where a correction demonstrably did not move the tool's verdict, so no pick is lost to an arbitrary count. Termination rests on the runner comparing Error: lines across calls, a per-block memory the orchestrating prose otherwise avoids holding, and a runner whose corrections keep producing new but different slips is still unbounded in principle; the rule is also the hardest of the set to state tersely in the skill.

A bounded number of corrected re-send calls (one, or until a call makes no progress), after which a block still refused ends the run on a failure report instead of a skip: the run prints the Short Title with the tool's Error: line verbatim in place of a success line, with everything already embedded staying committed by the earlier batched calls. A persistent refusal, which signals a runner or tool defect rather than a judgment call, is surfaced loudly instead of reading as a successful run with an advisory a headless chain's operator may overlook. It reverses design claim 15's "never a run stop" for an outcome that self-heals anyway (the block still lacks a recommendation, so the next run picks it), and turns a partly successful run into a reported failure although every other pick landed and committed.

open-question.question: When a run has no block to write, because every block already carried a recommendation or every candidate was skipped for having no surviving option, how does it still reach the fixed end-of-run sort and its Question-ordering commit: by running the same batched shell call with no block in it, or by a sort step kept in a form of its own for that case?
open-question.recommendation: One fixed call run exactly as shown on every run that found questions, the zero-pick run being the degenerate batch with no block section; its annotation commit is conditioned on a non-empty body, so an uncommitted change left by an interrupted run cannot be committed as an empty-bodied annotation, and the sort-and-commit lines exist once, so nothing can drift between two forms.
open-question.alternative: A zero-pick run runs the same fixed batched shell call as every other run, with its per-block embed-and-lift section repeated zero times: the annotation part writes and lifts nothing, its commit step finds nothing to commit, and the call goes on to sort and commit the reorder under Question-ordering exactly as a full run does. The skill shows one call and has no branch for the case. One mechanism for every run: the sort-and-commit lines exist once, the zero-pick run is just the degenerate batch, and every run that found questions reaches the sort through the same single call, so nothing can drift between two forms. The shown call must stay well-formed with no block section in it, and its annotation commit then runs with nothing lifted: under the plain dirty-own-path guard an uncommitted change already in open_questions.xml (an earlier run interrupted after an embed) would be committed as Recommendation-annotation with an empty body, unless the call conditions that commit on at least one lifted line. How safe this is depends on the form the Commit body capture question settles for the lifted lines and on how the Status line source question reads which commits landed.

The skill shows the batched call as two fixed sections, an annotation section (the embeds, the lifts, the Recommendation-annotation commit) followed by a sort section (sort, then the commit procedure's steps for Question-ordering). A run with picks runs both sections as one call. A zero-pick run runs the sort section alone as a shell call of its own. The sort text is written once and used by both. A zero-pick run never runs an annotation commit at all, so an empty-body Recommendation-annotation commit cannot happen, and the sort-and-commit text still exists once, so the two cases cannot drift apart. The runner builds a call from two shown pieces instead of running one call exactly as shown, which departs from the milestone 43 single-fixed-call precedent and adds a branch the runner can get wrong: a full run that drops the sort section skips the sort silently.

Beside the batched call, the skill shows a second complete fixed shell call for the zero-pick case: sort, then the commit procedure's three steps written literally for Question-ordering, with no embed, lift, or annotation commit. Each call is run exactly as shown, and the sort-and-commit lines appear in both. Each call is complete and run exactly as shown, as in the milestone 43 precedent, and the zero-pick script is short and holds no annotation machinery that would have to tolerate an empty block list. The sort-and-commit lines are duplicated in the skill, and so in all three host trees and in the docs that restate the pass, so an edit to one copy can leave the other stale. The skill also grows by a second script that exists only for the rarer case.

A zero-pick run keeps today's step 6 for that case: it runs sort as its own tool call and carries out the shared commit procedure for Question-ordering in the runner's own turns. Only runs with picks use the batched shell call, which sorts and commits itself. No sort-only shell script exists. It changes the least: the zero-pick path is today's tested wording, no new script is authored for it, and the extra turns it costs fall only on runs that wrote nothing, which are cheap already. The same sort-and-commit is done by two mechanisms depending on the case, so the skill, CLAUDE.md, and docs must describe both. The runner holds whether the ordering commit landed on one path while the call reports it on the other, which the Status line source question then has to cover twice. Zero-pick runs also keep paying the per-step turns the milestone sets out to remove.

A zero-pick run skips the sort and its Question-ordering commit entirely and goes straight to the report, printing the no-op line. Sorting happens only inside the batched call, which only runs when at least one block was picked. This reverses the current rule that the sort is a fixed end-of-run step on every run that found questions. The batched call only ever exists with blocks in it, so there is no empty-batch case, no second form, and no tool call at all after the gather on a run that has nothing to write. A document whose order went stale without a write in this run stays unsorted until some later run writes a block. Stale orders come from a recommendation stripped by an answer cascade or a goal revision, or from an earlier run whose sort failed. Walk computes its own order, so the answer sweep is unaffected, but readers of the document meet blocks out of walk order, and a deliberate end-of-run guarantee of the current skill is given up.

open-question.question: Once the batched shell call makes the Recommendation-annotation and Question-ordering commits itself, from what does the runner learn which of those commits landed, in order to choose between the two success lines and the no-op line of the report step?
open-question.recommendation: The commit facts are read in the same turn from the call that made the commits, with no extra tool call, no git-history read, no per-block ledger across re-sends, and no unstable git summary to scan; a guard that fired prints no marker, so the runner still never tests the sort outcome itself, and the three report lines stay true to the git log.
open-question.alternative: Source: the batched call's own print. Besides its failure lines, the call prints one fixed, identifier-free marker line each time one of its commits lands, one for the Recommendation-annotation commit and one for the Question-ordering commit. It prints the second only when the dirty-own-path guard let the sort's commit through. Git's success output stays silenced. The runner reads the markers across every batch call of the run, re-send calls included, and picks the report line in the existing strict order. The report keeps its three lines. The commit facts come from the same call that made the commits and are read in the same turn, so no extra tool call is needed and no outcome is inferred. A guard that fired leaves no marker, which keeps the step-7 rule that the runner never tests the sort outcome itself. The milestone 43 precedent is a call that prints nothing when everything succeeded, and this departs from it by adding two success-path lines that the call's prose has to define and the runner has to tell apart from failure lines. In a run that writes no block, the reorder line depends on the sort running inside a batch call, which is the axis the "Sort with nothing written" question owns.

Source: git's own output, left visible inside the batched call. The call runs git commit without -q and without capturing its output, so every landed commit prints git's summary line naming its subject, and a guard that fired prints nothing. The runner looks for the Recommendation-annotation and Question-ordering subjects in the combined print of every batch call in the run. The report keeps its three lines. No marker vocabulary of the pass's own is added. The evidence is git's own statement of the commit, so the status line stays tied to the git log, the record its strict order exists to match. The call needs no extra printf. Git's human-readable commit summary is not a stable interface: it includes the branch name and short hash and is followed by file-statistics lines, so the print the runner must scan grows and runs mixed with the call's failure lines. It also reverses milestone 43's choice to silence git's success output.

Source split by commit. The runner infers whether the annotation commit landed from what it already holds: the blocks it sent in each call, minus the blocks the call printed as refused, minus any failed-commit line. A block that went through and committed means the commit landed. Only the sort's commit is reported positively, as one fixed marker line the call prints when that commit lands. Otherwise the call stays failure-only. The report keeps its three lines. The call stays close to milestone 43's silent-on-success shape. The one fact the runner cannot work out for itself, whether the guard let the sort commit through, is the only one the call has to print. Across a first call and its corrected re-sends, the runner has to keep a per-block ledger of what it sent and what each call refused, and an error in that ledger turns into a wrong status line with nothing to check it against. How refused blocks are tied to titles is owned by the "Refused block print pairing" question, and what the tool prints per accepted block is owned by the "Multi-block embed tool form" question. Both bear on how easy the inference is.

Source split by commit, with a closing check modelled on the alternatives pass. After the last batch call, the runner runs list --without-recommendation once. If an id from the step-1c set is missing from that print, the run annotated something, and the runner prints Recommendations embedded. The sort's commit is reported as one fixed marker line the call prints when that commit lands, and the runner reads that marker only when the closing check shows no annotation. Otherwise the call stays failure-only. The report keeps its three lines. The two annotating passes would choose their status lines the same way, from the document as it ends up, and the result holds however many re-send calls the run made, with no per-block bookkeeping. It adds one tool call per run, in a milestone whose purpose is cutting post-decision turns. The check also reads document state rather than git, so an embed that wrote but whose commit git refused still counts as annotated. Only the failed-commit line catches that. The reorder line still needs the call to run the sort in a no-block run, which is the axis the "Sort with nothing written" question owns.

Source: git history, read after the run. Before the first batch call, the runner records the current HEAD commit with git rev-parse HEAD and keeps that one hash as a value. After the last batch call, it runs one path-scoped git log of the subjects committed since that hash to the milestone's open_questions.xml. It picks the report line in the existing strict order from the subjects present. Every batch call stays failure-only and silent on success, as in milestone 43. The report keeps its three lines. The status line is read straight from the git log it must stay true to. That covers every batch call of the run at once, including commits made by re-send calls, and the call script and its print contract stay unchanged. It adds two tool calls per run, one before and one after, and the runner must hold the start hash across calls. That works against the milestone's turn-cutting aim, and it brings a git-history read into a pass that has never needed one.

Rejects the premise that the run must tell all three lines apart. The report step drops the distinction between a reorder and no change: a run with no annotation commit prints one line that says no new recommendations were embedded, whether or not the sort committed. A run with an annotation commit prints Recommendations embedded. The runner needs only the annotation fact, taken from the call's failure-only print and what it sent, and the call carries no sort marker. The CLAUDE.md terse-reporting invariant and the step-7 wording are updated to match. The sort's guard outcome never has to reach the runner, so the batched call stays as silent and simple as milestone 43's and the report step gets shorter. The no-op line no longer promises that the run left git history untouched, since a Question-ordering commit can now land under it. It also changes a recorded invariant, under which recommend-all-open-questions is the one pass with two success lines chosen by what the run committed, for a saving that applies only to runs that write no block.
